concept_html:
Databricks pipelines mix PySpark with Spark SQL. The examples use Spark 4.0 SQL. Run SQL from Python with spark.sql("SELECT ..."), which returns a DataFrame.

Read and filter. SELECT region, final_weight FROM respondents WHERE final_weight > 0 picks columns and keeps rows.

Summarise. GROUP BY region makes one row per region. Aggregates work per group: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(final_weight) counts non-NULL values, and SUM and AVG skip NULLs. HAVING SUM(final_weight) > 100 filters groups after they are summarised, where WHERE filters rows before.

Join. JOIN regions g ON r.region_code = g.region_code keeps only matching rows. LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table and fills the right side with NULL when there is no match. LEFT ANTI JOIN keeps the left rows that have no match, which finds orphan keys in one line.

NULL means unknown. Any comparison with NULL is unknown, never true, so WHERE final_weight = NULL matches nothing. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL.

Pick one row per key. A delivery can repeat a respondent. A window function numbers the rows within each key, newest first, and you keep number 1:

SELECT respondent_id, wave_id, final_weight
FROM (
  SELECT *,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY respondent_id, wave_id ORDER BY delivery_version DESC) AS rn
  FROM bronze_deliveries
)
WHERE rn = 1

PARTITION BY sets the groups, ORDER BY ... DESC puts the newest first, and ROW_NUMBER() gives exactly one row the number 1 in each group. DISTINCT would keep both versions, because their values differ.

Lessons A3 and A4 add MERGE, GRANT and row filters on top of these.

title: The SQL that pipelines use
why_html: A data-quality check counted missing weights with WHERE final_weight = NULL. It reported zero every night for two months while 1,800 weights were missing, because a comparison with NULL is never true. IS NULL found them on the first run, and the check now catches the problem it was written for.
